question_html: Under section 88(1), which registers is every company required to keep and maintain?

options.A: Register of Members, Register of Debenture-holders, and Register of any other security holders
options.B: Only a Register of Members; registers of debenture-holders and other security holders are optional and may be maintained at the company's discretion
options.C: Only a Register of Directors and Key Managerial Personnel; registers of members, debenture-holders, and other security holders are governed exclusively by SEBI regulations, not the Companies Act, 2013
options.D: Only a Register of Charges; registers of members, debenture-holders, and other security holders are subsumed within the Register of Charges under Chapter VI

answer_html:
Correct answer: (A) Register of Members, Register of Debenture-holders, and Register of any other security holders

Section 88(1) requires every company to keep and maintain a Register of Members, a Register of Debenture-holders, and a Register of any other security holders - each in the prescribed form (Form MGT-1 for members under Rule 3, Form MGT-2 for debenture-holders/other security holders under Rule 4).

question_html: Under Rule 5(1), within what period must entries be made in the register of members (or the respective register) following approval by the Board or a committee thereof of an allotment or transfer of shares, debentures, or other securities?

options.A: Within 30 days of the date of approval by the Board or the committee thereof, mirroring the timeline for registration of a charge
options.B: Within 7 days of the date of approval by the Board or the committee thereof
options.C: Within 24 hours of the date of approval by the Board or the committee thereof, with no grace period at all

answer_html:

question_html: Under Rule 5(2), where must the registers (of members, debenture-holders, or other security holders) ordinarily be maintained, and under what condition may they be kept elsewhere?

options.A: The registers shall always be maintained at the office of the Registrar of Companies, and never at the company's own registered office, regardless of any resolution passed by the company
options.B: The registers may be kept at any place in India the Board of Directors considers convenient, by ordinary resolution alone, with no requirement of a special resolution or any locational nexus to where members reside
options.C: The registers shall be maintained at the registered office of the company, unless a special resolution is passed in a general meeting authorising the keeping of the register at any other place within the city, town, or village in which the registered office is situated, or any other place in India in which more than one-tenth of the total members entered in the register of members reside
options.D: The registers must always be maintained at the registered office, with no exception permitting any other location under any circumstances, even with shareholder approval by special resolution

answer_html:
Correct answer: (C) The registers shall be maintained at the registered office of the company, unless a special resolution is passed in a general meeting authorising the keeping of the register at any other place within the city, town, or village in which the registered office is situated, or any other place in India in which more than one-tenth of the total members entered in the register of members reside

Rule 5(2) requires the registers to be maintained at the registered office, unless a special resolution authorises keeping them elsewhere - either within the city/town/village of the registered office, or at any other place in India where more than one-tenth of the total members (per the register of members) reside.

question_html: Under section 88(4) read with Rule 7, may a company keep a part of its register of members (or debenture-holders/other security holders) in a country outside India, and what filing obligation arises upon opening such a register?

options.A: No - the Companies Act, 2013 categorically prohibits any company from maintaining any part of its register of members outside India under any circumstances, regardless of what its articles provide
options.B: Yes, but only with the prior approval of the Reserve Bank of India (and not merely authorisation by the company's own articles), and no notice to the Registrar of Companies is required at any stage
options.C: Yes, if so authorised by its articles, but such a Foreign Register is treated as an entirely separate and independent register, NOT deemed to be part of the company's principal register, for any purpose under the Act
options.D: Yes, if so authorised by its articles, a company may keep, in any country outside India, a part of the register of members (or debenture-holders/other security holders/beneficial owners) resident in that country, called a 'Foreign Register' (deemed part of the company's 'principal register'); the company must, within 30 days from the date of opening any Foreign Register, file with the Registrar a notice of the situation of the office where such register is kept, in Form No. MGT-3 along with the requisite fee

answer_html:
Correct answer: (D) Yes, if so authorised by its articles, a company may keep, in any country outside India, a part of the register of members (or debenture-holders/other security holders/beneficial owners) resident in that country, called a 'Foreign Register' (deemed part of the company's 'principal register'); the company must, within 30 days from the date of opening any Foreign Register, file with the Registrar a notice of the situation of the office where such register is kept, in Form No. MGT-3 along with the requisite fee

Section 88(4) (read with Rule 7) permits a company, if authorised by its articles, to keep a Foreign Register in a country outside India for members/debenture-holders/other security holders/beneficial owners resident there - deemed part of the company's principal register. Within 30 days of opening any Foreign Register, the company must file notice of its situation with the Registrar in Form No. MGT-3, along with the requisite fee.

question_html: While a transaction with respect to shares, debentures, or other securities remains registered in a Foreign Register, can it also be registered in any other register of the company? And within what period must a copy of every entry made in a Foreign Register be transmitted to the company's registered office in India?

options.A: No transaction with respect to any shares, debentures, or other security registered in a Foreign Register shall, during the continuance of that registration, be registered in any other register; the company shall transmit to its registered office in India a copy of every entry in any Foreign Register within 15 days after the entry is made
options.B: The same transaction may be simultaneously and independently registered in both the Foreign Register and the principal register maintained in India, with no restriction against dual registration
options.C: No transaction may ever be registered in a Foreign Register at all; only the principal register maintained in India carries any legal effect under the Companies Act, 2013
options.D: The company must transmit a copy of every entry in the Foreign Register to its registered office in India within 60 days after the entry is made, mirroring the timeline for filing of the annual return

answer_html:
Correct answer: (A) No transaction with respect to any shares, debentures, or other security registered in a Foreign Register shall, during the continuance of that registration, be registered in any other register; the company shall transmit to its registered office in India a copy of every entry in any Foreign Register within 15 days after the entry is made

The Study Material specifies that no transaction registered in a Foreign Register shall, during the continuance of that registration, also be registered in any other register - avoiding duplicate/conflicting entries. The company must transmit a copy of every entry made in any Foreign Register to its registered office in India within 15 days after the entry is made, keeping a duplicate Foreign Register (itself deemed part of the principal register) updated at the registered office.

question_html: What penalty applies if a company does not maintain a register of members, debenture-holders, or other security holders, or fails to maintain them in accordance with section 88(1) or 88(2), and what is the nature of this offence?

options.A: The company shall be liable to a penalty of Rs. 30 lakh, and every officer in default shall be liable to imprisonment for up to 3 years, with no possibility of compounding under section 441
options.B: The company shall be liable to a penalty of Rs. 3 lakh, and every officer of the company who is in default shall be liable to a penalty of Rs. 50,000; the offence is a compoundable offence under section 441 of the Act
options.C: The company alone shall be liable to a penalty of Rs. 5 lakh, with no separate penalty prescribed for officers of the company who are in default
options.D: The company shall be liable to a penalty of Rs. 1 lakh, and every officer in default shall be liable to a penalty of Rs. 3 lakh - i.e., the reverse of the correct allocation between company and officer

answer_html:
Correct answer: (B) The company shall be liable to a penalty of Rs. 3 lakh, and every officer of the company who is in default shall be liable to a penalty of Rs. 50,000; the offence is a compoundable offence under section 441 of the Act

Failure to maintain a register of members/debenture-holders/other security holders in accordance with section 88(1)/(2) attracts a penalty of Rs. 3 lakh on the company and Rs. 50,000 on every officer in default - and this is expressly a compoundable offence under section 441 of the Companies Act, 2013.

question_html: Under section 89(1) and (2), what declarations must be filed, in what forms, and within what timelines, where a registered holder of shares does not hold the beneficial interest in them?

options.A: Both the registered owner and the beneficial owner must file identical declarations in Form No. MGT-6, within 90 days of the relevant event, with no distinction in form or timeline between the two categories
options.B: Only the beneficial owner is required to make any declaration at all (in Form No. MGT-5, within 60 days); the registered owner has no corresponding declaration obligation under section 89
options.C: The registered owner must file a declaration in Form No. MGT-4 with the company, specifying the beneficial owner's particulars, within 30 days from the date his name is entered in the register of members; every person who holds/acquires a beneficial interest in shares must make a declaration to the company in Form No. MGT-5, within 30 days after acquiring such beneficial interest
options.D: The registered owner must file Form No. MGT-5 within 15 days, and the beneficial owner must file Form No. MGT-4 within 15 days - i.e., the forms and the applicable declarant are reversed

answer_html:
Correct answer: (C) The registered owner must file a declaration in Form No. MGT-4 with the company, specifying the beneficial owner's particulars, within 30 days from the date his name is entered in the register of members; every person who holds/acquires a beneficial interest in shares must make a declaration to the company in Form No. MGT-5, within 30 days after acquiring such beneficial interest

Section 89(1) (with Rule 9(1)) requires the registered owner (whose name is entered in the register but who lacks beneficial interest) to declare, in Form MGT-4, the beneficial owner's particulars, within 30 days of his name being entered in the register. Section 89(2) (with Rule 9(2)) requires the beneficial owner himself to declare, in Form MGT-5, the nature of his interest and the registered holder's particulars, within 30 days of acquiring the beneficial interest.

question_html: Where a declaration under section 89 is made to a company, what must the company do, and what is the consequence if a beneficial owner fails to make the required declaration at all?

options.A: The company has no obligation to file anything with the Registrar; and non-filing of the declaration by the beneficial owner has no consequence at all on the enforceability of his rights in the shares
options.B: The company must file a return in Form No. MGT-4 (the same form used by the registered owner) with the Registrar, within 90 days; non-filing merely triggers a warning letter, with the beneficial owner's rights remaining fully enforceable
options.C: The company must file the return within 30 days, but in Form No. MGT-5 (the beneficial owner's own declaration form); non-filing of the beneficial owner's declaration only suspends his voting rights, while his right to dividend remains fully enforceable
options.D: The company must note the declaration in the relevant register and file a return in Form No. MGT-6 with the Registrar, within 30 days from the date of receipt of the declaration, along with the fee; if the required declaration is not made by the beneficial owner, any right with respect to those shares shall NOT be enforceable by the beneficial owner or by any person claiming through him

answer_html:
Correct answer: (D) The company must note the declaration in the relevant register and file a return in Form No. MGT-6 with the Registrar, within 30 days from the date of receipt of the declaration, along with the fee; if the required declaration is not made by the beneficial owner, any right with respect to those shares shall NOT be enforceable by the beneficial owner or by any person claiming through him

Section 89(6) (with Rule 9(3)) requires the company, on receiving a section 89 declaration, to note it in the register and file a return in Form MGT-6 with the Registrar within 30 days of receipt, with fee. Section 89(8) provides that where the beneficial owner fails to make the required declaration, ANY right with respect to those shares (not merely voting or dividend rights) shall not be enforceable by him or by any person claiming through him.

question_html: Under section 89(10), what does 'beneficial interest' in a share include, for the purposes of sections 89 and 90?

options.A: Directly or indirectly, through any contract, arrangement, or otherwise, the right or entitlement of a person - alone or together with any other person - to exercise or cause to be exercised any or all of the rights attached to the share, OR to receive or participate in any dividend or other distribution in respect of the share
options.B: Only the right to physically hold the share certificate in one's own custody, regardless of any right to exercise voting rights or receive dividends attached to the share
options.C: Only formal legal ownership of the share as recorded in the register of members, entirely excluding any economic or voting interest exercised through a contract or arrangement
options.D: Only the right to sell or transfer the share to a third party, excluding any right to exercise voting rights or receive dividends or other distributions in respect of the share

answer_html:
Correct answer: (A) Directly or indirectly, through any contract, arrangement, or otherwise, the right or entitlement of a person - alone or together with any other person - to exercise or cause to be exercised any or all of the rights attached to the share, OR to receive or participate in any dividend or other distribution in respect of the share

Section 89(10) defines 'beneficial interest' broadly (for both sections 89 and 90) to include, directly or indirectly through any contract/arrangement/otherwise, a person's right or entitlement (alone or with others) to exercise or cause to be exercised rights attached to the share, or to receive/participate in any dividend or other distribution - encompassing both the voting/control dimension and the economic dimension of share ownership.

question_html: Under section 90(1), a significant beneficial owner (SBO) is an individual holding beneficial interest of not less than what percentage in a company's shares, or exercising significant influence/control - and how does Rule 2(1)(h) of the SBO Rules operationalise this?

options.A: Section 90(1) sets the threshold at exactly 51%, requiring outright majority ownership before any individual can be treated as a significant beneficial owner, with no lower prescribed threshold under the SBO Rules
options.B: Section 90(1) sets the threshold at not less than 25% (or such other percentage as may be prescribed) of beneficial interest, or the right to exercise/actual exercise of significant influence or control; Rule 2(1)(h) of the Companies (Significant Beneficial Owners) Rules, 2018 operationalises this by treating a person as an SBO where he holds (indirectly, or indirectly together with direct holdings) not less than 10% of shares, voting rights, or the right to participate in distributable dividend, or exercises significant influence/control other than through direct holdings alone
options.C: Section 90(1) sets the threshold at 10%, and the SBO Rules subsequently raised this operative threshold to 25% for all categories of holding, direct and indirect alike
options.D: Section 90(1) applies only to listed companies, and the SBO Rules extend the concept for the first time to unlisted companies at an entirely different (and undefined) threshold

answer_html:
Correct answer: (B) Section 90(1) sets the threshold at not less than 25% (or such other percentage as may be prescribed) of beneficial interest, or the right to exercise/actual exercise of significant influence or control; Rule 2(1)(h) of the Companies (Significant Beneficial Owners) Rules, 2018 operationalises this by treating a person as an SBO where he holds (indirectly, or indirectly together with direct holdings) not less than 10% of shares, voting rights, or the right to participate in distributable dividend, or exercises significant influence/control other than through direct holdings alone

Section 90(1)'s statutory language sets a 25%-or-prescribed-percentage threshold, but Rule 2(1)(h) of the SBO Rules, 2018 (exercising the 'or such other percentage as may be prescribed' power) operationalises the actual reporting threshold at 10% - covering indirect holding of shares, voting rights, or dividend participation, or the exercise of significant influence/control otherwise than through direct holdings alone - so an individual crossing 10% on an indirect (or indirect-plus-direct) basis is treated as an SBO in practice.

question_html: Under section 91(1), for what maximum aggregate period in a year, and for what maximum period at any one time, may a company close its register of members, debenture-holders, or other security holders, and what minimum notice must be given?

options.A: A company may close such registers for an aggregate period of 45 days in each year, but not exceeding 30 days at any one time; the registers may be closed by giving a minimum of 7 days' notice, or such lesser period as SEBI may specify for listed companies or those intending to get their securities listed
options.B: A company may close such registers for an aggregate period of 90 days in each year, but not exceeding 60 days at any one time, with a minimum notice period of 21 days in every case
options.C: A company may close such registers indefinitely, for any period it considers appropriate, without any statutory ceiling on either the aggregate or the single-instance closure period
options.D: A company may close such registers for an aggregate period of 15 days in each year, but not exceeding 5 days at any one time, with no minimum notice period prescribed at all

answer_html:

question_html: Under section 91(2), what penalty applies where a company closes its registers without giving notice, after giving a shorter notice than prescribed, or for a period exceeding the specified aggregate/single-instance limits?

options.A: The company alone (and not any officer) shall be liable to a flat penalty of Rs. 1,00,000, with the offence being non-compoundable under any circumstances
options.B: The company and every officer of the company who is in default shall be liable to a penalty of Rs. 5,000 per day, subject to a maximum of Rs. 1,00,000, during which the register is kept closed - and the offence is compoundable under section 441
options.C: The company and every officer in default shall be liable to imprisonment for up to 6 months, with no monetary penalty prescribed at all under section 91(2)
options.D: The company and every officer in default shall be liable to a penalty of Rs. 50,000 per day, with no prescribed maximum ceiling on the aggregate penalty

question_html: Under section 94(1), where must the registers kept under section 88 and copies of the annual return filed under section 92 ordinarily be kept, and what evidentiary status do these registers, indices, and copies of annual return carry under section 95?

options.A: They must always be kept at the office of the Registrar of Companies, and under section 95, they carry no evidentiary value whatsoever in any legal proceeding
options.B: They must always be kept at the registered office with no exception permitting any other location, and under section 95, they constitute conclusive (not merely prima facie) evidence of every matter they contain
options.C: They shall ordinarily be kept at the registered office of the company (though they may also be kept at any other place in India where more than one-tenth of the total members reside, if approved by special resolution); under section 95, the registers, indices, and copies of annual return shall be prima facie evidence of any matter directed or authorised to be inserted therein by or under the Act

question_html: Who must sign the Annual Return of an ordinary company (not an OPC or small company), and in which cases must the Annual Return additionally be certified by a Company Secretary in practice (in Form No. MGT-8)?

options.A: The Annual Return may be signed by any shareholder of the company, and certification by a Company Secretary in practice is mandatory for every company without exception, regardless of its listing status, paid-up capital, or turnover
options.B: The Annual Return shall be signed by a director of the company and the company secretary (or, if there is no company secretary, by a company secretary in practice); it must additionally be certified by a Company Secretary in practice, in Form No. MGT-8, where the company is a LISTED company, OR has a paid-up share capital of Rs. 10 crore or more, OR a turnover of Rs. 50 crore or more

options.D: The Annual Return must be signed by the statutory auditor of the company (not a director or company secretary), and certification by a Company Secretary in practice applies only to Government companies

question_html: Under section 92(4), within what period must a copy of the Annual Return be filed with the Registrar, and does the obligation to file persist even where the AGM was not actually held in a given year?

options.A: The obligation to file the Annual Return is entirely suspended for any year in which the AGM is not actually held, with no fallback filing deadline or reason-disclosure requirement under section 92(4)
options.B: A copy of the Annual Return must be filed within 90 days from the date the AGM is held, and there is no fallback provision at all for a year in which the AGM was not held
options.C: A copy of the Annual Return must be filed within 30 days from the date the AGM is held, and where no AGM is held, the company is permanently exempted from filing any Annual Return for that year
options.D: A copy of the Annual Return must be filed with the Registrar within 60 days from the date the AGM is held; where no AGM is held in any year, it shall be filed within 60 days from the date the AGM SHOULD HAVE been held, along with the reasons for not holding the AGM - the obligation to file persists regardless of whether the AGM actually took place

answer_html:

question_html: What penalty applies under section 92(5) for a company's failure to file its Annual Return in time, and under section 92(6) for a Company Secretary in practice who certifies the Annual Return otherwise than in accordance with section 92 or the rules?

options.A: A notice of at least 14 clear days is required for every company without exception, with section 8 companies additionally required to give 21 days' notice as a heightened, not reduced, requirement

question_html: Under the proviso to section 101(1), a general meeting may be called after giving shorter notice than 21 clear days, if consent is accorded by what proportion of members - and does this threshold differ between an AGM and any other general meeting?

options.A: The threshold is identical for both an AGM and any other general meeting: a flat 95% of the paid-up share capital carrying voting rights, with no separate headcount-based requirement for either category of meeting
options.B: For an AGM, only a simple majority (more than 50%) of members entitled to vote is required; for other general meetings, unanimous (100%) consent of all members is required, regardless of their paid-up capital
options.C: The threshold for an AGM is 90% of members entitled to vote, and for other general meetings, 90% of the paid-up share capital carrying voting rights - both lower than the actual 95% figures prescribed
options.D: For an AGM, consent of not less than 95% of the members entitled to vote thereat is required; for any other general meeting (of a company having share capital), consent is required from members holding a majority in number of those entitled to vote AND who represent not less than 95% of such part of the paid-up share capital as gives a right to vote at the meeting (or, for a company without share capital, not less than 95% of the total voting power)

answer_html:
Correct answer: (D) For an AGM, consent of not less than 95% of the members entitled to vote thereat is required; for any other general meeting (of a company having share capital), consent is required from members holding a majority in number of those entitled to vote AND who represent not less than 95% of such part of the paid-up share capital as gives a right to vote at the meeting (or, for a company without share capital, not less than 95% of the total voting power)

The proviso to section 101(1) distinguishes AGM shorter-notice consent (95% of MEMBERS entitled to vote - a headcount-only threshold) from other-general-meeting shorter-notice consent (majority in NUMBER of members entitled to vote, AND those members representing not less than 95% of the voting paid-up share capital - a dual, number-plus-value threshold) - as illustrated by the Aakash Soaps Limited example, where 60% of members (a majority) holding shares worth only 80% (not 95%) of paid-up capital failed to meet the dual threshold.

question_html: Under section 102, when must an 'Explanatory Statement' be annexed to the notice calling a general meeting, and what must it specify?

options.A: Where any special business is to be transacted at the general meeting, an Explanatory Statement must be annexed to the notice, specifying: the nature of concern or interest (financial or otherwise), if any, of every director, manager, and other KMP, and their relatives, in respect of each item of business; and any other information/facts enabling members to understand the meaning, scope, and implications of the items of business and take a decision thereon

question_html: Which four matters are recognised as 'ordinary business' at an Annual General Meeting, and what is the status of business transacted at an Extraordinary General Meeting?

options.A: The four ordinary business items are: appointment of the Managing Director, alteration of the memorandum, buy-back of shares, and reduction of capital - all other business at an AGM is special business, and business at an EGM is never treated as special business
options.B: The four ordinary business items are: consideration of financial statements and the reports of the Board and auditors; declaration of any dividend; appointment of directors in place of those retiring; and appointment of, and fixing the remuneration of, the auditors - all other business at an AGM is 'special business', and at an EGM, EVERY item of business transacted is special business

question_html: Under section 102(4), if non-disclosure or insufficient disclosure in the Explanatory Statement results in a benefit accruing to a promoter, director, manager, KMP, or their relative, what is the consequence for that person?

options.A: No consequence at all arises for the person who received the benefit; section 102(4) is a purely declaratory provision with no substantive remedy for the company
options.B: The benefit automatically reverts, by operation of law, to the shareholder who raised the objection personally, rather than to the company as a whole
options.C: Such person shall hold the benefit received in trust for the company, and shall (without prejudice to any other action against him under the Act or any other law) be liable to compensate the company to the extent of the benefit he received
options.D: The person who received the benefit becomes automatically disqualified from being a director of any company for a period of five years, this being the sole consequence prescribed by section 102(4)

question_html: If the quorum is not present within half an hour from the time appointed for holding a meeting, what happens, and what if quorum is also not present at the adjourned meeting?

options.A: The meeting shall stand adjourned to the same day in the next week, at the same time and place, or to such other date/time/place as the Board may determine (with at least 3 days' notice of any change of day/time/place); however, a meeting called by requisitionists under section 100 shall instead stand cancelled if quorum is not present; where quorum is also not present at the adjourned meeting, the members present shall themselves form the quorum
options.B: The meeting is automatically and permanently cancelled in every case, with no possibility of an adjourned meeting under any circumstances, regardless of who called the original meeting
options.C: The meeting must be immediately reconvened later on the very same day, with no possibility of adjournment to a future date; if quorum is again absent, the company is wound up
options.D: The meeting stands adjourned indefinitely with no fixed adjourned date at all, and the 'members present form the quorum' rule never applies even at a further adjourned meeting

question_html: Under section 104, unless the articles otherwise provide, how is the Chairman of a meeting elected, and when does the Chairman have a 'casting vote'?

options.A: The Chairman is always appointed by the Registrar of Companies, never elected by the members, and always has an automatic casting vote regardless of what the articles provide
options.B: Unless the articles provide otherwise, the members personally present shall elect one among themselves to be the Chairman, on a show of hands; the Chairman has a casting vote (a right to cast a second vote in the event of equality of votes) in Board and general meetings ONLY if specifically empowered by the articles of the company - absent such a provision, a resolution on which votes are equal is deemed dropped
options.C: The Chairman is always the company's Managing Director by default, with no election process at all, and never has any casting vote under any circumstances, articles notwithstanding
options.D: The members elect the Chairman by postal ballot only, never by show of hands, and the Chairman's casting vote is available automatically in every case without needing any express articles-based empowerment

answer_html:
Correct answer: (B) Unless the articles provide otherwise, the members personally present shall elect one among themselves to be the Chairman, on a show of hands; the Chairman has a casting vote (a right to cast a second vote in the event of equality of votes) in Board and general meetings ONLY if specifically empowered by the articles of the company - absent such a provision, a resolution on which votes are equal is deemed dropped

Section 104 provides that, absent contrary articles, members personally present elect their own Chairman by show of hands (with the elected Chairman continuing until superseded by a poll-elected Chairman, if a poll on the Chairman's election is demanded). The Chairman's 'casting vote' (a second, tie-breaking vote) is available only if the ARTICLES specifically empower it - without such empowerment, an equally-voted ordinary resolution is deemed dropped rather than passed by the Chairman's casting vote.

question_html: Under section 105(1), what right does a member entitled to attend and vote at a meeting have regarding appointment of a proxy, and what are the limitations on a proxy's participation?

options.A: A proxy has exactly the same rights as the member himself, including an unrestricted right to speak at the meeting and to vote on a show of hands as well as on a poll
options.B: Only a member holding more than 50% of the company's paid-up share capital is entitled to appoint a proxy; smaller shareholders have no statutory right to appoint a proxy at all
options.C: Any member entitled to attend and vote at a meeting is entitled to appoint another person as a proxy to attend and vote at the meeting on his behalf; however, a proxy shall NOT have the right to speak at the meeting, and shall NOT be entitled to vote except on a poll
options.D: A proxy may speak at the meeting on any item of business, but has no right to vote at all, whether on a show of hands or on a poll, under any circumstances

answer_html:
Correct answer: (C) Any member entitled to attend and vote at a meeting is entitled to appoint another person as a proxy to attend and vote at the meeting on his behalf; however, a proxy shall NOT have the right to speak at the meeting, and shall NOT be entitled to vote except on a poll

question_html: Under Rule 19(2), what is the maximum number of members (and aggregate shareholding) for whom a single person may act as proxy, and what exception applies to a member holding more than 10% of the company's total voting share capital?

options.A: A person can act as proxy for an unlimited number of members, provided their aggregate shareholding does not exceed 25% of the company's total voting share capital, with no exception for members holding more than 10%
options.B: A person can act as proxy for a maximum of 10 members, holding in aggregate not more than 50% of the company's total voting share capital, and there is no special provision at all for members holding a large shareholding
options.C: A person can act as proxy for a maximum of 100 members regardless of their aggregate shareholding, with a member holding more than 10% required to appoint at least two separate proxies rather than a single one
options.D: A person can act as proxy on behalf of members not exceeding 50, and holding in aggregate not more than 10% of the total share capital of the company carrying voting rights; however, a member holding MORE than 10% of the total voting share capital may appoint a single person as proxy, and that person shall not act as proxy for any OTHER person or shareholder

answer_html:

question_html: Under section 105(4), what is the effect where a company's articles require an instrument of proxy to be deposited more than 48 hours before a meeting?

options.A: A proxy received 48 hours before the meeting will be valid even if the articles provide for a longer period - the articles' 'longer than 48 hours' requirement takes effect as if 48 hours had been specified instead
options.B: The articles' longer deposit period (e.g., 72 hours) prevails absolutely, and a proxy deposited only 48 hours before the meeting is invalid if the articles require a longer period
options.C: Section 105(4) has no bearing at all on articles-based deposit-timing requirements; the articles' stipulated period always governs, however long it may be
options.D: A proxy must be deposited at least 96 hours (double the statutory minimum) before the meeting in every case, regardless of what shorter or longer period the articles may specify

answer_html:
Correct answer: (A) A proxy received 48 hours before the meeting will be valid even if the articles provide for a longer period - the articles' 'longer than 48 hours' requirement takes effect as if 48 hours had been specified instead

Section 105(4) caps the effective proxy-deposit deadline at 48 hours before the meeting - even where a company's articles purport to require a longer period (e.g., 72 hours), such a provision takes effect only as if 48 hours had been specified, protecting members from an unreasonably early cut-off imposed by the articles.

question_html: Under section 106(1) and (2), on what grounds (and only those grounds) may a company's articles validly restrict a member's voting rights?

options.A: The articles may restrict voting rights on any ground the Board considers appropriate, including a member's personal conduct, professional background, or political affiliation, with no statutory limitation on permissible grounds
options.B: The articles may provide that no member shall exercise voting rights in respect of any share on which any amount is due from him on calls or other sums presently payable to the company, or in regard to which the company has exercised any right of lien; a company shall NOT prohibit any member from exercising voting rights on ANY OTHER ground
options.C: The articles may never restrict voting rights under any circumstances, even for unpaid calls or a lien exercised by the company, since section 106 is an absolute guarantee of unrestricted voting for every member
options.D: The articles may restrict voting rights only where a member has been convicted of an offence under any law, with unpaid calls and company liens being expressly excluded as permissible restriction grounds

answer_html:
Correct answer: (B) The articles may provide that no member shall exercise voting rights in respect of any share on which any amount is due from him on calls or other sums presently payable to the company, or in regard to which the company has exercised any right of lien; a company shall NOT prohibit any member from exercising voting rights on ANY OTHER ground

Section 106(1) permits articles-based voting restrictions ONLY on two grounds: unpaid calls/other presently-payable sums, or an exercised right of lien. Section 106(2) is an exhaustiveness provision - a company cannot prohibit voting on ANY OTHER ground - so, absent an articles provision on these two specific grounds, a member cannot be prevented from voting even if calls remain unpaid or a lien has been exercised.

question_html: Under section 107, unless a poll or electronic voting is demanded, in what manner is a resolution first voted upon at a meeting, and what evidentiary status does the Chairman's declaration of the result (by show of hands) carry?

options.A: Voting by show of hands is available only as a last resort, after both a poll and electronic voting have already been demanded and conducted; the Chairman's declaration carries no evidentiary weight at all
options.B: Voting by show of hands is the default first mode, but the Chairman's declaration is merely rebuttable (prima facie) evidence, capable of being displaced by evidence that the vote count was, in fact, different
options.C: Voting shall be done by way of show of hands in the first instance (section 107(1)); the Chairman's declaration of the passing (or otherwise) of a resolution by show of hands, and an entry to that effect in the minutes book, shall be CONCLUSIVE EVIDENCE that the resolution has been passed (or not passed), per section 107(2)
options.D: Voting by show of hands has been entirely abolished by the Companies Act, 2013, with electronic voting being the sole permissible mode of voting at any company meeting

answer_html:
Correct answer: (C) Voting shall be done by way of show of hands in the first instance (section 107(1)); the Chairman's declaration of the passing (or otherwise) of a resolution by show of hands, and an entry to that effect in the minutes book, shall be CONCLUSIVE EVIDENCE that the resolution has been passed (or not passed), per section 107(2)

Section 107(1) makes show of hands the default first-instance voting mode (unless a poll/e-voting is demanded). Section 107(2) makes the Chairman's declaration of the show-of-hands result (plus the corresponding minutes-book entry) CONCLUSIVE (not merely prima facie) evidence that the resolution was passed or not passed - a stronger evidentiary status than that accorded generally to registers/returns under section 95.

question_html: Under section 109, in the case of a company having a share capital, what threshold must members present in person or by proxy satisfy in order to validly demand a poll?

options.A: The members demanding a poll must hold, in aggregate, not less than 1/3rd of the total voting power AND shares on which at least Rs. 50,00,000 has been paid up - both conditions must be met cumulatively
options.B: Only a single member, however small his shareholding, may demand a poll in every case, with no minimum voting-power or paid-up-value threshold prescribed under section 109
options.C: The members demanding a poll must hold, in aggregate, not less than 1/2 of the total voting power, this being the sole threshold prescribed under section 109 for a company having share capital
options.D: The members demanding a poll must hold, in aggregate, not less than 1/10th of the total voting power, OR shares on which an aggregate sum of not less than Rs. 5,00,000 (or such higher amount as may be prescribed) has been paid up - satisfying EITHER threshold is sufficient

answer_html:
Correct answer: (D) The members demanding a poll must hold, in aggregate, not less than 1/10th of the total voting power, OR shares on which an aggregate sum of not less than Rs. 5,00,000 (or such higher amount as may be prescribed) has been paid up - satisfying EITHER threshold is sufficient

question_html: Under Rule 22 (pursuant to section 110(1)(a)), which of the following is correctly recognised as an item of business that must be transacted only by means of postal ballot, and which companies are exempted from the postal ballot requirement altogether?

options.A: Alteration of the objects clause of the memorandum; buy-back of shares under section 68(1); variation in rights attached to a class of shares/debentures/securities under section 48; and election of a director under section 151 are among the items requiring compulsory postal ballot; One Person Companies and companies having members up to 200 are NOT required to transact any business through postal ballot

question_html: Under Rule 22, within what period from dispatch of the notice must a shareholder's assent or dissent by postal ballot be received, and what is the effect under section 110(2) if the resolution is assented to by the requisite majority?

options.A: The shareholder's assent or dissent must be sent within 90 days of dispatch, and even if assented to by the requisite majority, the resolution is NOT deemed to have been passed at a general meeting - a further confirmatory physical meeting is always mandatory
options.B: The shareholder's assent or dissent must be sent within a period of 30 days from the date of dispatch of the notice (any reply received thereafter is treated as if no reply was received); if the resolution is assented to by the requisite majority of shareholders by postal ballot, it shall be DEEMED to have been duly passed at a general meeting convened in that behalf
options.C: The shareholder's assent or dissent must be sent within 7 days of dispatch, and the resolution can never be validly passed through postal ballot alone, irrespective of the majority obtained
options.D: The shareholder's assent or dissent must be sent within 15 days of dispatch, and the deeming provision under section 110(2) applies only to ordinary resolutions, never to special resolutions

answer_html:
Correct answer: (B) The shareholder's assent or dissent must be sent within a period of 30 days from the date of dispatch of the notice (any reply received thereafter is treated as if no reply was received); if the resolution is assented to by the requisite majority of shareholders by postal ballot, it shall be DEEMED to have been duly passed at a general meeting convened in that behalf

Rule 22 fixes a 30-day window (from dispatch of the postal ballot notice) for shareholders to return their assent/dissent, with late replies disregarded. Section 110(2) creates a deeming fiction: a resolution assented to by the requisite majority via postal ballot is deemed to have been duly passed at a general meeting convened for that purpose - dispensing with any further physical-meeting confirmation, and applying equally to ordinary and special resolutions.

question_html: Under section 111(2), which of the following is a prerequisite for a valid requisition by members seeking circulation of a proposed resolution (and any accompanying statement) under section 111?

options.A: The requisition may be made orally by any single member, with no minimum shareholding threshold, and no deposit of expenses is required under any circumstances
options.B: The requisition must be signed by members holding not less than one-half of the paid-up voting share capital, and must be deposited not less than six months before the meeting in every case, without exception
options.C: The requisition must be made in writing and signed by such number of members holding not less than one-tenth of the paid-up voting share capital (or, for a no-share-capital company, one-tenth of total voting power); it must be deposited at the registered office not less than six weeks before the meeting (for a resolution requiring notice) or not less than two weeks before the meeting (for other resolutions); and a sum reasonably sufficient to meet the company's expenses in giving effect to the resolution must be deposited or tendered

answer_html:
Correct answer: (C) The requisition must be made in writing and signed by such number of members holding not less than one-tenth of the paid-up voting share capital (or, for a no-share-capital company, one-tenth of total voting power); it must be deposited at the registered office not less than six weeks before the meeting (for a resolution requiring notice) or not less than two weeks before the meeting (for other resolutions); and a sum reasonably sufficient to meet the company's expenses in giving effect to the resolution must be deposited or tendered

question_html: Under section 114, what majority of votes cast is required for a resolution to be an 'ordinary resolution', and what majority is required for a 'special resolution'?

options.A: An ordinary resolution requires votes in favour to be at least twice the votes against; a special resolution requires votes in favour to be at least 3 times the votes against - i.e., the ordinary-resolution majority is overstated
options.B: Both an ordinary resolution and a special resolution require exactly the same majority: votes in favour must simply exceed votes against, with no distinction in the required ratio between the two categories

Per Secretarial Standard-2, can Mr. Rustom, being treated as 4 'members present' for quorum purposes, single-handedly satisfy the quorum requirement for Meadowfield Industries Limited (which, with 4,200 members, requires a quorum of 15) without any other individual present?

options.A: Yes - since Mr. Rustom is deemed to be 4 members present by virtue of representing 4 body corporate members, and 4 is less than 15 in any event, quorum computation is irrelevant to this question
options.B: Yes - Secretarial Standard-2 imposes no minimum on the number of distinct individuals physically present, so long as the aggregate 'members present' figure (however computed) reaches the quorum threshold
options.C: No, but only because Meadowfield Industries Limited's quorum threshold (15) exceeds the number of bodies corporate Mr. Rustom represents (4); had he represented at least 15 bodies corporate, he could have satisfied quorum alone
options.D: No - although one person can be an authorised representative of more than one body corporate (and is treated as more than one member present for quorum purposes), Secretarial Standard-2 requires that AT LEAST TWO INDIVIDUALS be present in person to constitute a meeting; a lone authorised representative, however many bodies corporate he represents, cannot by himself satisfy this two-individual minimum

answer_html:
Correct answer: (D) No - although one person can be an authorised representative of more than one body corporate (and is treated as more than one member present for quorum purposes), Secretarial Standard-2 requires that AT LEAST TWO INDIVIDUALS be present in person to constitute a meeting; a lone authorised representative, however many bodies corporate he represents, cannot by himself satisfy this two-individual minimum

Per Secretarial Standard-2's clarificatory note, one person can be an authorised representative of more than one body corporate and is counted as more than one member present for quorum - BUT to constitute a meeting at all, at least two individuals must be physically present. Mr. Rustom alone, however many bodies corporate he represents, cannot single-handedly satisfy quorum without at least one more individual (a member, proxy-appointing member present in person, or another representative) also being physically present.

Can Northgate Chemicals Limited validly call its AGM on shorter notice, having obtained consent from members representing only 92% (by headcount, of members entitled to vote thereat)?

options.A: Yes - the AGM shorter-notice threshold is 90% (not 95%) of members entitled to vote, and 92% comfortably exceeds this correct threshold
options.B: No - the proviso to section 101(1) requires, for an AGM, consent of not less than 95% of the MEMBERS entitled to vote thereat (a headcount-based threshold, not a paid-up-capital-based one); 92% falls short of this 95% threshold, so the AGM cannot be validly called on shorter notice on this consent
options.C: Yes - the relevant AGM threshold under section 101(1) is expressed in terms of paid-up share capital value (not member headcount), and 92% of paid-up capital value would suffice regardless of the number of members consenting
options.D: No, but only because the consent was not accorded in writing (electronic-mode consent being invalid for an AGM); had it been given in writing, 92% would have sufficed

answer_html:
Correct answer: (B) No - the proviso to section 101(1) requires, for an AGM, consent of not less than 95% of the MEMBERS entitled to vote thereat (a headcount-based threshold, not a paid-up-capital-based one); 92% falls short of this 95% threshold, so the AGM cannot be validly called on shorter notice on this consent

For an AGM, the proviso to section 101(1) requires consent of not less than 95% of the MEMBERS entitled to vote thereat - a pure headcount threshold, distinct from the dual number-plus-value threshold applicable to other general meetings. question_html:
Northgate Chemicals Limited has a paid-up share capital of Rs. 90 lakh divided into 9 lakh equity shares of Rs. 10 each (each carrying one vote). For its upcoming Annual General Meeting, the Board wishes to give shorter notice than the statutory 21 clear days, and obtains written consent from members entitled to vote holding, in aggregate, shares representing 92% of the members entitled to vote thereat (by headcount). Separately, for an Extraordinary General Meeting to consider an unrelated matter, the Board obtains consent (by electronic mode) from 58% of the members in number (a majority), who together hold shares worth Rs. 86,40,000 (i.e., 96% of the Rs. 90 lakh paid-up share capital).

Can Northgate Chemicals Limited validly call its EGM on shorter notice, having obtained consent from 58% of members in number (a majority) holding shares worth Rs. 86,40,000 (96% of paid-up capital)?

options.A: No - the EGM shorter-notice threshold requires 95% of members BY NUMBER (not merely a majority), and 58% falls far short of this correct 95% headcount requirement
options.B: No - since only 96% (not the full paid-up capital) has consented, and section 101(1) for an EGM requires 100% consent by value, the threshold has not been met
options.C: Yes - for a general meeting other than an AGM (in the case of a company having share capital), the proviso to section 101(1) requires consent from members holding a majority in number of those entitled to vote AND representing not less than 95% of the paid-up voting share capital; 58% of members (a majority) holding 96% of paid-up capital (exceeding 95%) satisfies BOTH limbs of this dual threshold
options.D: Yes, but only because Northgate Chemicals Limited is a private company; had it been a public company, a materially higher consent percentage would have been required for an EGM

answer_html:
Correct answer: (C) Yes - for a general meeting other than an AGM (in the case of a company having share capital), the proviso to section 101(1) requires consent from members holding a majority in number of those entitled to vote AND representing not less than 95% of the paid-up voting share capital; 58% of members (a majority) holding 96% of paid-up capital (exceeding 95%) satisfies BOTH limbs of this dual threshold

For a general meeting other than an AGM (company having share capital), the proviso to section 101(1) requires: majority in NUMBER of members entitled to vote, AND those members must represent not less than 95% of the paid-up share capital carrying voting rights. Here, 58% of members (comfortably a majority) hold Rs. 86,40,000 out of Rs. 90,00,000 paid-up capital, i.e., 96% - exceeding the 95% value threshold - so both limbs of the dual test are satisfied, unlike the Aakash Soaps Limited illustration in the Study Material where the 95% value limb was not met.

question_html:
Riverside Textiles Limited held its Annual General Meeting attended by 80 members entitled to vote. A resolution was proposed to be passed as a special resolution. Of the 80 members present, 15 voted against the resolution and 10 abstained from voting altogether; the remaining members voted in favour. Separately, at the same meeting, a different item of ordinary business (not the special resolution) was first put to vote by show of hands; 20 members present in person, holding in aggregate shares on which only Rs. 3,00,000 has been paid up (representing less than 1/10th of Riverside Textiles Limited's total voting power), then demanded that this item instead be decided by poll.

Was the special resolution validly passed at Riverside Textiles Limited's AGM, given that 15 members voted against, 10 abstained, and the remaining 55 members (80 - 15 - 10) voted in favour?

options.A: Yes - under section 114(2), a special resolution requires votes in favour to be not less than 3 times the votes cast against (here, 3 x 15 = 45 votes required in favour, at minimum); 55 votes in favour comfortably exceeds this 45-vote threshold, so the resolution was validly passed as a special resolution
options.B: No - since 10 members abstained, the resolution automatically fails to qualify as a special resolution, regardless of the numerical relationship between votes cast in favour and against
options.C: No - a special resolution requires unanimous consent of all 80 members present, and since 15 voted against and 10 abstained, unanimity was not achieved, so the resolution failed
options.D: Yes, but only because the total attendance (80 members) exceeded the section 103 quorum requirement for a public company; the favour-to-against vote ratio is not independently relevant under section 114(2)

answer_html:
Correct answer: (A) Yes - under section 114(2), a special resolution requires votes in favour to be not less than 3 times the votes cast against (here, 3 x 15 = 45 votes required in favour, at minimum); 55 votes in favour comfortably exceeds this 45-vote threshold, so the resolution was validly passed as a special resolution

Section 114(2) requires votes in favour of a special resolution to be not less than 3 times the votes cast against it - abstentions are simply excluded from the computation (as in the Super Star Bakers Limited illustration). Here, 15 votes against requires a minimum of 45 votes in favour; the actual 55 votes in favour (80 total members, less 15 against, less 10 abstaining) comfortably clears this threshold, so the special resolution was validly passed.

Separately, at the same meeting, a different item of ordinary business (not the special resolution) was first put to vote by show of hands; 20 members present in person, holding in aggregate shares on which only Rs. 3,00,000 has been paid up (representing less than 1/10th of Riverside Textiles Limited's total voting power), then demanded that this item instead be decided by poll.

Is the demand for a poll (on the separate item of ordinary business), made by 20 members holding in aggregate less than 1/10th of the total voting power and only Rs. 3,00,000 of paid-up value, a valid demand under section 109?

options.A: Yes - since 20 is a reasonably large number of members in absolute terms, section 109 is satisfied by headcount alone, regardless of their aggregate voting power or paid-up shareholding value
options.B: No - section 109 requires, for a company having share capital, that the demanding members hold EITHER not less than 1/10th of the total voting power OR shares on which an aggregate of not less than Rs. 5,00,000 has been paid up; here, neither threshold is met (voting power is below 1/10th, and paid-up value is only Rs. 3,00,000, short of Rs. 5,00,000), so the poll demand is invalid
options.C: Yes - meeting either the 1/10th voting-power test or holding shares worth Rs. 3,00,000 or more (a lower threshold than Rs. 5,00,000) is sufficient under section 109, so the demand is valid on the paid-up-value limb alone
options.D: No, but only because the item in question is ordinary (not special) business; poll demands are available only in respect of special business under section 109, irrespective of the members' voting power or shareholding value

answer_html:
Correct answer: (B) No - section 109 requires, for a company having share capital, that the demanding members hold EITHER not less than 1/10th of the total voting power OR shares on which an aggregate of not less than Rs. 5,00,000 has been paid up; here, neither threshold is met (voting power is below 1/10th, and paid-up value is only Rs. 3,00,000, short of Rs. 5,00,000), so the poll demand is invalid

Section 109 requires, for a company with share capital, that members demanding a poll hold not less than 1/10th of the total voting power OR shares with an aggregate paid-up value of not less than Rs. 5,00,000 (whichever threshold is met suffices). Here, the demanding members satisfy neither: their voting power is below 1/10th, and their aggregate paid-up value (Rs. 3,00,000) falls short of the Rs. 5,00,000 floor - so the poll demand is invalid, and voting by show of hands would stand (subject to the Chairman's own discretion to order a poll on his own motion under section 109).

Suppose, hypothetically, that instead of being voted on at the physical AGM, Riverside Textiles Limited's special resolution had instead been assented to by the requisite majority of shareholders entirely through postal ballot. Would such a resolution be treated as validly passed?

options.A: No - a resolution can never be validly passed solely through postal ballot; postal ballot outcomes are merely advisory and must always be ratified by a subsequent vote at a physical general meeting
options.B: No - postal ballot is available only for ordinary resolutions, never for special resolutions, so a special resolution assented to by postal ballot alone would be invalid regardless of the majority obtained
options.C: Yes - under section 110(2), if a resolution is assented to by the requisite majority of shareholders by means of postal ballot, it shall be DEEMED to have been duly passed at a general meeting convened in that behalf - it carries the same legal effect as a resolution passed at a physical meeting, without needing any further confirmatory meeting
options.D: Yes, but only if the postal ballot process is conducted at the same physical venue and on the same date as the AGM it purports to substitute; a wholly separate postal ballot process carries no legal effect

answer_html:
Correct answer: (C) Yes - under section 110(2), if a resolution is assented to by the requisite majority of shareholders by means of postal ballot, it shall be DEEMED to have been duly passed at a general meeting convened in that behalf - it carries the same legal effect as a resolution passed at a physical meeting, without needing any further confirmatory meeting

Section 110(2) creates an express deeming provision: a resolution assented to by the requisite majority of shareholders via postal ballot is deemed to have been duly passed at a general meeting convened for that purpose - conferring full legal effect without requiring any further physical-meeting ratification, and applying to both ordinary and special resolutions transacted by postal ballot.

question_html:
Coral Bay Engineering Limited (an unlisted company, not a One Person Company or a small company) has a paid-up share capital of Rs. 12 crore and an annual turnover of Rs. 32 crore. It called its AGM to lay before shareholders the financial statements for the financial year ended 31st March, 2026, but the meeting could not proceed for want of quorum and was cancelled. Coral Bay Engineering's directors are of the view that, since the AGM did not actually take place, the 60-day period for filing the Annual Return under section 92(4) does not apply, and that the company is therefore under no obligation to file an Annual Return for that financial year at all.

Is the view of Coral Bay Engineering Limited's directors - that no Annual Return filing obligation arises because the AGM did not actually take place - correct?

options.A: Yes - the directors' view is correct; section 92(4) applies only where an AGM is actually held, and imposes no fallback filing obligation of any kind where the AGM does not take place
options.B: No, but only because Coral Bay Engineering Limited's paid-up capital exceeds Rs. 10 crore; a company with lower paid-up capital would indeed have no filing obligation if its AGM was not held
options.C: Yes, but only for the current financial year; the company would still be required to file its Annual Return for all subsequent financial years even if their AGMs are also not held
options.D: No - section 92(4) expressly provides that where no AGM is held in any year, the Annual Return shall be filed within 60 days from the date the AGM SHOULD HAVE been held, along with the reasons for not holding the AGM; the obligation to file the Annual Return persists regardless of whether the AGM actually took place, exactly as illustrated by the Big Fox Entertainment Limited example in the Study Material

answer_html:
Correct answer: (D) No - section 92(4) expressly provides that where no AGM is held in any year, the Annual Return shall be filed within 60 days from the date the AGM SHOULD HAVE been held, along with the reasons for not holding the AGM; the obligation to file the Annual Return persists regardless of whether the AGM actually took place, exactly as illustrated by the Big Fox Entertainment Limited example in the Study Material

The directors' view is incorrect. Section 92(4) squarely addresses the AGM-not-held scenario: the Annual Return must still be filed, within 60 days from the date the AGM should have been held, accompanied by reasons for not holding it. Non-filing on the (mistaken) premise that the AGM-not-held excuses the obligation itself constitutes a contravention of section 92, exposing the company to the section 92(5) penalty - precisely the analysis applied to Big Fox Entertainment Limited in the Study Material's own illustration.

question_html:
Coral Bay Engineering Limited (an unlisted company, not a One Person Company or a small company) has a paid-up share capital of Rs. 12 crore and an annual turnover of Rs. 32 crore. It called its AGM to lay before shareholders the financial statements for the financial year ended 31st March, 2026, but the meeting could not proceed for want of quorum and was cancelled. Coral Bay Engineering's directors are of the view that, since the AGM did not actually take place, the 60-day period for filing the Annual Return under section 92(4) does not apply, and that the company is therefore under no obligation to file an Annual Return for that financial year at all.

Given that Coral Bay Engineering Limited is unlisted and has a turnover of Rs. 32 crore (below Rs. 50 crore), but a paid-up share capital of Rs. 12 crore, must its Annual Return be certified by a Company Secretary in practice?

options.A: Yes - under section 92(2) read with Rule 11(2), certification by a Company Secretary in practice (in Form No. MGT-8) is required if the company is listed, OR has a paid-up share capital of Rs. 10 crore or more, OR has a turnover of Rs. 50 crore or more; Coral Bay Engineering's paid-up capital of Rs. 12 crore independently satisfies the second limb, even though it is unlisted and its turnover is below Rs. 50 crore
options.B: No - since Coral Bay Engineering Limited is unlisted and its turnover (Rs. 32 crore) is below Rs. 50 crore, certification is not required; the paid-up-capital criterion is relevant only for listed companies
options.C: No - certification by a Company Secretary in practice is required only where ALL THREE conditions (listed status, paid-up capital of Rs. 10 crore or more, AND turnover of Rs. 50 crore or more) are cumulatively satisfied, and Coral Bay Engineering fails two of the three
options.D: Yes, but only if Coral Bay Engineering Limited's Annual Return is filed more than 60 days late; timely filing within 60 days of the AGM (or the date it should have been held) would exempt it from any certification requirement

answer_html:
Correct answer: (A) Yes - under section 92(2) read with Rule 11(2), certification by a Company Secretary in practice (in Form No. MGT-8) is required if the company is listed, OR has a paid-up share capital of Rs. 10 crore or more, OR has a turnover of Rs. 50 crore or more; Coral Bay Engineering's paid-up capital of Rs. 12 crore independently satisfies the second limb, even though it is unlisted and its turnover is below Rs. 50 crore

Section 92(2)/Rule 11(2) triggers PCS certification on ANY ONE of three independent conditions being met: listed status, paid-up share capital of Rs. 10 crore or more, or turnover of Rs. 50 crore or more. Coral Bay Engineering's Rs. 12 crore paid-up capital independently crosses the Rs. 10 crore threshold, making certification mandatory regardless of its unlisted status and its turnover being below Rs. 50 crore - the three conditions operate disjunctively (via 'or'), not cumulatively.

case_facts_html: Coral Bay Engineering Limited (an unlisted company, not a One Person Company or a small company) has a paid-up share capital of Rs. 12 crore and an annual turnover of Rs. 32 crore. It called its AGM to lay before shareholders the financial statements for the financial year ended 31st March, 2026, but the meeting could not proceed for want of quorum and was cancelled. Coral Bay Engineering's directors are of the view that, since the AGM did not actually take place, the 60-day period for filing the Annual Return under section 92(4) does not apply, and that the company is therefore under no obligation to file an Annual Return for that financial year at all.
question_html:
Coral Bay Engineering Limited (an unlisted company, not a One Person Company or a small company) has a paid-up share capital of Rs. 12 crore and an annual turnover of Rs. 32 crore. It called its AGM to lay before shareholders the financial statements for the financial year ended 31st March, 2026, but the meeting could not proceed for want of quorum and was cancelled. Coral Bay Engineering's directors are of the view that, since the AGM did not actually take place, the 60-day period for filing the Annual Return under section 92(4) does not apply, and that the company is therefore under no obligation to file an Annual Return for that financial year at all.

In which form must Coral Bay Engineering Limited file its Annual Return, given that it is neither a One Person Company nor a small company?

options.A: Form No. MGT-7A - since Coral Bay Engineering Limited is unlisted, Rule 11 treats every unlisted company (not merely OPCs and small companies) as eligible for the abridged form
options.B: Form No. MGT-7 - the standard (non-abridged) Annual Return form applicable to every company except a One Person Company and a Small Company, which instead use the abridged Form No. MGT-7A
options.C: Form No. MGT-8 - since certification by a Company Secretary in practice is required (given its Rs. 12 crore paid-up capital), the Annual Return itself must be filed in the certification form MGT-8 rather than MGT-7
options.D: Form No. MGT-6 - since a return under section 89 may also be required of the company in respect of beneficial-interest declarations, the Annual Return itself is filed on the same Form No. MGT-6

answer_html:
Correct answer: (B) Form No. MGT-7 - the standard (non-abridged) Annual Return form applicable to every company except a One Person Company and a Small Company, which instead use the abridged Form No. MGT-7A

Rule 11 confines the abridged Form No. MGT-7A to a One Person Company and a Small Company; every other company (including an unlisted company like Coral Bay Engineering Limited, regardless of its paid-up capital or turnover) files its Annual Return in the standard Form No. MGT-7. Form MGT-8 is a separate certification document appended by the practising Company Secretary, not a substitute for the MGT-7 Annual Return itself; Form MGT-6 is the company's return relating to declarations of beneficial interest under section 89, an entirely distinct filing.

case_facts_html: A general meeting of Falcon Retail Ventures Limited was scheduled for Friday, 20th June, 2025, at 4:00 p.m. Member Priyansh appointed Ms. Devika as his proxy; the proxy form, dated 15th June, 2025, was deposited with the company at its registered office on 17th June, 2025. Separately, member Waheeda executed two separate proxy instruments in respect of the same meeting: one in favour of Mr. Salim, dated 18th June, 2025, deposited with the company at 2:00 p.m. on 18th June, 2025; and another in favour of Ms. Tanvi, dated 18th June, 2025, deposited with the company at 5:00 p.m. on 18th June, 2025 (i.e., after the first). Both Mr. Salim and Ms. Tanvi, along with Ms. Devika, were present at the meeting seeking to vote on Waheeda's and Priyansh's behalf, respectively.
question_html:
A general meeting of Falcon Retail Ventures Limited was scheduled for Friday, 20th June, 2025, at 4:00 p.m. Member Priyansh appointed Ms. Devika as his proxy; the proxy form, dated 15th June, 2025, was deposited with the company at its registered office on 17th June, 2025. Separately, member Waheeda executed two separate proxy instruments in respect of the same meeting: one in favour of Mr. Salim, dated 18th June, 2025, deposited with the company at 2:00 p.m. on 18th June, 2025; and another in favour of Ms. Tanvi, dated 18th June, 2025, deposited with the company at 5:00 p.m. on 18th June, 2025 (i.e., after the first). Both Mr. Salim and Ms. Tanvi, along with Ms. Devika, were present at the meeting seeking to vote on Waheeda's and Priyansh's behalf, respectively.

Is Ms. Devika's appointment as Priyansh's proxy validly deposited, given the meeting is at 4:00 p.m. on 20th June, 2025 (so the 48-hour cut-off falls at 4:00 p.m. on 18th June, 2025), and the proxy form was deposited on 17th June, 2025?

options.A: No - the proxy form is invalid because it was deposited on 17th June, 2025, which is MORE than 48 hours before the meeting; section 105(4) requires deposit to occur exactly at, and no earlier than, the 48-hour mark
options.B: No - since the proxy form is dated 15th June, 2025 (5 days before the meeting), and section 105(4) caps validity at exactly 48 hours' advance dating, the form is invalid for being dated too far in advance
options.C: Yes - the proxy form was deposited on 17th June, 2025, well before the 48-hour cut-off of 4:00 p.m. on 18th June, 2025 (48 hours prior to the 4:00 p.m. meeting on 20th June, 2025); under section 105(4), a proxy received 48 hours before the meeting is valid (and would remain valid even if the articles purported to require an earlier deposit)
options.D: Yes, but only because Ms. Devika is a member of Falcon Retail Ventures Limited in her own right; had she not been a member, her appointment as proxy would have been invalid irrespective of the deposit timing

answer_html:
Correct answer: (C) Yes - the proxy form was deposited on 17th June, 2025, well before the 48-hour cut-off of 4:00 p.m. on 18th June, 2025 (48 hours prior to the 4:00 p.m. meeting on 20th June, 2025); under section 105(4), a proxy received 48 hours before the meeting is valid (and would remain valid even if the articles purported to require an earlier deposit)

Section 105(4) establishes 48 hours before the meeting as the LATEST permissible deposit deadline (a ceiling, not a floor) - depositing earlier than 48 hours before the meeting (as Priyansh's proxy form was, on 17th June, well ahead of the 18th June 4:00 p.m. cut-off) is perfectly valid; there is no requirement that deposit occur AT, rather than before, the 48-hour mark, and a proxy need not himself be a member of the company.

Both Mr. Salim and Ms. Tanvi, along with Ms. Devika, were present at the meeting seeking to vote on Waheeda's and Priyansh's behalf, respectively.

As between Mr. Salim (proxy instrument deposited at 2:00 p.m. on 18th June, 2025, before the 4:00 p.m. cut-off) and Ms. Tanvi (proxy instrument deposited at 5:00 p.m. on 18th June, 2025, after the cut-off), both appointed by Waheeda for the same meeting, who is entitled to vote on Waheeda's behalf?

options.A: Ms. Tanvi is entitled to vote, since her proxy instrument is dated later and therefore supersedes the earlier instrument in favour of Mr. Salim, on the general legal principle that the most recent instrument governs
options.B: Neither Mr. Salim nor Ms. Tanvi is entitled to vote, since Waheeda's appointment of two competing proxies for the same meeting automatically invalidates both instruments in their entirety
options.C: Both Mr. Salim and Ms. Tanvi are entitled to vote simultaneously on Waheeda's behalf, each exercising half of her voting entitlement, since both instruments were lodged on the same calendar date
options.D: Mr. Salim is entitled to vote on Waheeda's behalf - where two proxy instruments by the same shareholder are lodged such that one is lodged before, and the other after, the expiry of the date/time fixed for lodging proxies (the 48-hour cut-off), the FORMER (the timely instrument, in favour of Mr. Salim) is counted, and Ms. Tanvi's later-lodged instrument is disregarded

answer_html:
Correct answer: (D) Mr. Salim is entitled to vote on Waheeda's behalf - where two proxy instruments by the same shareholder are lodged such that one is lodged before, and the other after, the expiry of the date/time fixed for lodging proxies (the 48-hour cut-off), the FORMER (the timely instrument, in favour of Mr. Salim) is counted, and Ms. Tanvi's later-lodged instrument is disregarded

Where a shareholder lodges two proxy instruments for the same meeting - one before, and one after, expiry of the proxy-lodging deadline - the FORMER (timely) instrument is the one that counts. Since Mr. Salim's instrument was deposited at 2:00 p.m. on 18th June (before the 4:00 p.m. cut-off) and Ms. Tanvi's was deposited at 5:00 p.m. (after the cut-off), Mr. Salim is entitled to vote on Waheeda's behalf, and Ms. Tanvi's later instrument is disregarded.

Both Mr. Salim and Ms. Tanvi, along with Ms. Devika, were present at the meeting seeking to vote on Waheeda's and Priyansh's behalf, respectively.

Was it permissible, in principle, for Waheeda to execute two separate proxy instruments (in favour of Mr. Salim and Ms. Tanvi respectively) for the same meeting, before considering which instrument ultimately prevails?

options.A: Yes - section 105(2) itself contemplates that, where the articles allow, a member may appoint 'one or more proxies' to attend and vote instead of himself; a member may accordingly execute multiple proxy instruments for the same meeting, though (per the timely-lodging rule) only the instrument validly and timely deposited within the 48-hour window will ultimately be recognised as effective
options.B: No - the Companies Act, 2013 permits a member to appoint only a single proxy for any given meeting under all circumstances, so Waheeda's execution of two separate instruments was itself impermissible and rendered both instruments void from the outset
options.C: No - appointing more than one proxy is permissible only for a private company, and since Falcon Retail Ventures Limited's classification is not stated, the appointment must be presumed invalid
options.D: Yes, but only where the member concerned holds more than 10% of the company's total voting share capital, this being the sole basis on which multiple proxy appointments by a single member are permitted

answer_html:
Correct answer: (A) Yes - section 105(2) itself contemplates that, where the articles allow, a member may appoint 'one or more proxies' to attend and vote instead of himself; a member may accordingly execute multiple proxy instruments for the same meeting, though (per the timely-lodging rule) only the instrument validly and timely deposited within the 48-hour window will ultimately be recognised as effective

Section 105(2) expressly contemplates 'one or more proxies' (where the articles so allow) as part of the compliance statement required in meeting notices - so a member may in principle appoint more than one proxy for the same meeting. The practical resolution of competing instruments from the same member is governed by the timely-lodging rule (the instrument deposited within the 48-hour window prevails over one deposited after that window), not by an outright prohibition on multiple appointments.
