case_facts_html: Solstice Renewables Limited is the 'Reporting Company' for the purposes of the Companies (Significant Beneficial Owners) Rules, 2018. Mr. Devraj holds no shares directly in his own name in Solstice Renewables, but indirectly holds 12% of its shares through Meridian Holdings Private Limited (a body corporate through which Mr. Devraj exercises control). Solstice Renewables, upon investigation, has reasonable cause to believe that Ms. Fiza (who is not herself a member of Solstice Renewables) has knowledge of the identity of a significant beneficial owner of the company, and accordingly issues her a notice in Form No. BEN-4, calling upon her to furnish the relevant information within the time specified in the notice (30 days from the date of the notice, per Rule 7). Ms. Fiza does not respond to the notice at all within that specified time.
question_html:
Solstice Renewables Limited is the 'Reporting Company' for the purposes of the Companies (Significant Beneficial Owners) Rules, 2018. Mr. Devraj holds no shares directly in his own name in Solstice Renewables, but indirectly holds 12% of its shares through Meridian Holdings Private Limited (a body corporate through which Mr. Devraj exercises control). Solstice Renewables, upon investigation, has reasonable cause to believe that Ms. Fiza (who is not herself a member of Solstice Renewables) has knowledge of the identity of a significant beneficial owner of the company, and accordingly issues her a notice in Form No. BEN-4, calling upon her to furnish the relevant information within the time specified in the notice (30 days from the date of the notice, per Rule 7). Ms. Fiza does not respond to the notice at all within that specified time.

Is Mr. Devraj, holding 12% of Solstice Renewables Limited's shares indirectly (through Meridian Holdings, with no direct holding of his own), treated as a 'significant beneficial owner' under the Companies (Significant Beneficial Owners) Rules, 2018?

options.A: No - since Mr. Devraj holds no shares directly in his own name, he can never be treated as a significant beneficial owner under the SBO Rules, regardless of the extent of his indirect holding through Meridian Holdings
options.B: Yes - Rule 2(1)(h) of the SBO Rules treats an individual as an SBO where he holds indirectly (or indirectly together with any direct holding) not less than 10% of the shares of the reporting company; Mr. Devraj's 12% indirect holding (through Meridian Holdings) exceeds this 10% operative threshold, so he is an SBO, notwithstanding that section 90(1)'s own statutory text refers to a 25% (or prescribed) threshold
options.C: No - the SBO Rules apply a flat 25% indirect-holding threshold (mirroring section 90(1)'s own statutory language exactly), and Mr. Devraj's 12% indirect holding falls short of this 25% mark
options.D: Yes, but only if Mr. Devraj additionally holds an equivalent direct shareholding in Solstice Renewables Limited; a purely indirect holding, however large, can never independently trigger SBO status under the Rules

answer_html:
Correct answer: (B) Yes - Rule 2(1)(h) of the SBO Rules treats an individual as an SBO where he holds indirectly (or indirectly together with any direct holding) not less than 10% of the shares of the reporting company; Mr. Devraj's 12% indirect holding (through Meridian Holdings) exceeds this 10% operative threshold, so he is an SBO, notwithstanding that section 90(1)'s own statutory text refers to a 25% (or prescribed) threshold

Rule 2(1)(h) of the SBO Rules operationalises the SBO concept at a 10% threshold for indirect holdings (or indirect holdings combined with any direct holding) of shares, voting rights, or dividend-participation rights - lower than section 90(1)'s own '25% or prescribed percentage' statutory language, since the Rules exercise the delegated power to prescribe 'such other percentage'. Mr. Devraj's 12% indirect holding through Meridian Holdings independently crosses this 10% threshold, making him an SBO despite having no direct shareholding of his own.

Since Ms. Fiza fails to respond to the BEN-4 notice within the 30-day period specified in it, within what period must Solstice Renewables Limited apply to the Tribunal, and for what kind of order?

options.A: Solstice Renewables must apply to the Tribunal within 60 days of the expiry of the notice period, seeking an order compulsorily winding up the company, this being the sole remedy available under section 90(7)
options.B: Solstice Renewables has no obligation to approach the Tribunal at all; a non-response to a BEN-4 notice under the SBO Rules carries no further consequence beyond the notice itself
options.C: Solstice Renewables must apply to the Tribunal within 15 days of the expiry of the period specified in the notice (i.e., within 15 days after the 30-day BEN-4 response window lapses), for an order directing that the shares in question be subject to restrictions - such as restriction on transfer of interest, suspension of the right to receive dividend/other distribution, suspension of voting rights, or any other restriction on rights attached to the shares
options.D: Solstice Renewables must apply to the Tribunal within 15 days, but only for an order directing Ms. Fiza's arrest, since section 90(7) is a purely criminal (not civil-restriction) remedy

answer_html:
Correct answer: (C) Solstice Renewables must apply to the Tribunal within 15 days of the expiry of the period specified in the notice (i.e., within 15 days after the 30-day BEN-4 response window lapses), for an order directing that the shares in question be subject to restrictions - such as restriction on transfer of interest, suspension of the right to receive dividend/other distribution, suspension of voting rights, or any other restriction on rights attached to the shares

Section 90(7) requires the company to apply to the Tribunal within 15 days of expiry of the period specified in the BEN-4 notice (30 days, per Rule 7), where the addressee fails to give the required information (or gives unsatisfactory information) - seeking an order under Rule 7 restricting the shares in question: transfer restrictions, suspension of dividend/other distribution rights, suspension of voting rights, or any other restriction on the rights attached to the shares.

Coverage includes Chapter VII of the Companies Act, 2013 (sections 88 to 122) and the Companies (Management and Administration) Rules, 2014: registers of members, debenture-holders and other security holders under section 88, the foreign register, declaration of beneficial interest in shares under section 89, the register of significant beneficial owners under section 90 (read with the Companies (Significant Beneficial Owners) Rules, 2018), the power to close the register of members/debenture-holders/other security holders under section 91, the place of keeping and inspection of registers and returns under section 94 and their evidentiary value under section 95, the annual return under section 92 (contents, signing, certification, filing timeline and penalties), notice of meetings under section 101, the explanatory statement under section 102, quorum under section 103 and the chairman of meetings under section 104, proxies under section 105, restrictions on voting rights and the modes of voting (show of hands, electronic means, poll) under sections 106 to 109, postal ballot under section 110, circulation of members' resolutions under section 111, ordinary and special resolutions and other resolution-related provisions under sections 114 to 117, minutes under section 118 and their inspection under section 119, the annual general meeting under section 96 (and the Tribunal's power to call one under section 97), extraordinary general meetings under section 100, and the special provisions applicable to a One Person Company under section 122.

subject: Corporate and Other Laws
case_facts_html: Solstice Renewables Limited is the 'Reporting Company' for the purposes of the Companies (Significant Beneficial Owners) Rules, 2018. Mr. Devraj holds no shares directly in his own name in Solstice Renewables, but indirectly holds 12% of its shares through Meridian Holdings Private Limited (a body corporate through which Mr. Devraj exercises control). Solstice Renewables, upon investigation, has reasonable cause to believe that Ms. Fiza (who is not herself a member of Solstice Renewables) has knowledge of the identity of a significant beneficial owner of the company, and accordingly issues her a notice in Form No. BEN-4, calling upon her to furnish the relevant information within the time specified in the notice (30 days from the date of the notice, per Rule 7). Ms. Fiza does not respond to the notice at all within that specified time.
question_html:
Solstice Renewables Limited is the 'Reporting Company' for the purposes of the Companies (Significant Beneficial Owners) Rules, 2018. Mr. Devraj holds no shares directly in his own name in Solstice Renewables, but indirectly holds 12% of its shares through Meridian Holdings Private Limited (a body corporate through which Mr. Devraj exercises control). Solstice Renewables, upon investigation, has reasonable cause to believe that Ms. Fiza (who is not herself a member of Solstice Renewables) has knowledge of the identity of a significant beneficial owner of the company, and accordingly issues her a notice in Form No. BEN-4, calling upon her to furnish the relevant information within the time specified in the notice (30 days from the date of the notice, per Rule 7). Ms. Fiza does not respond to the notice at all within that specified time.

Assuming the Tribunal makes a restriction order under section 90(8) in respect of the shares connected to Ms. Fiza's non-response, what happens if neither Solstice Renewables Limited nor any aggrieved person applies for relaxation or lifting of the restrictions within one year of the date of that order?

options.A: The restrictions imposed by the Tribunal's order automatically and permanently continue forever, with no possibility of the shares ever being transferred to any authority or person, even after the passage of decades
options.B: The shares are automatically cancelled and the company's paid-up share capital is correspondingly reduced, without any order of the Tribunal or compliance with the capital-reduction provisions under section 66
options.C: The restricted shares automatically vest in the Central Government (not the Investor Education and Protection Fund Authority) after one year, to be held on trust for eventual identification of the true significant beneficial owner
options.D: If no application for relaxation or lifting of the restrictions has been filed within one year from the date of the Tribunal's order, those shares shall be transferred, without any restrictions, to the authority constituted under section 125(5) of the Companies Act, 2013 (i.e., the Investor Education and Protection Fund Authority), in the manner as may be prescribed

answer_html:
Correct answer: (D) If no application for relaxation or lifting of the restrictions has been filed within one year from the date of the Tribunal's order, those shares shall be transferred, without any restrictions, to the authority constituted under section 125(5) of the Companies Act, 2013 (i.e., the Investor Education and Protection Fund Authority), in the manner as may be prescribed

Section 90(9) permits the company or an aggrieved person to apply to the Tribunal for relaxation/lifting of section 90(8) restrictions, within one year of the date of the Tribunal's order. If no such application is filed within that one-year window, the restricted shares shall be transferred, WITHOUT any restrictions, to the authority constituted under section 125(5) - the Investor Education and Protection Fund (IEPF) Authority - in the manner prescribed, rather than remaining perpetually restricted or reverting to the company itself.
